newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - JAPANESE LIFE.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - JAPANESE LIFE.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
The failure last Friday of Japanese life insurer Nissan Mutual, the first such failure in the country in 50 years, has sent shock waves across the region.

Nissan got into trouble after guaranteeing returns to policy- and pension-holders of up to 5.5 per cent - a practice matched by most of Japan's 18 other life insurance firms. However as Japanese interest rates plummeted, Nissan became committed to an excess of outflow of interest instead of an inflow of interest gains.
In addition to a cash flow crisis, Nissan was estimated to have accumulates a deficit of around USD1.6 billion over the past three or four years, largely from poor performing investments.

The insurance industry has responded to the Nissan collapse with a 200 billion Yen policyholder protection fund, of which the top five insurers, Nippon Life, Dai-ichi Mutual, Sumitomo Life, Meiji Mutual and Asahi Mutual Life, will have to shoulder 60 per cent. They hope it will be enough to meet the bill.

The low interest rates pose a problem to all Japanese life insurers, which together manage USD144 trillion, although analysts believe the bigger ones can fall back on unrealised capital gains which in Japan are kept off the balance sheet.

But the crackdown by the Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) in putting Nissan into liquidation may signal an end to the paternalistic attitude which it has previously shown towards financial institutions.

For years it has been taken as gospel that guaranteed promises from the life insurance companies would have the protection of the MOF in the event of failure. But the conclusion now being drawn from the MOF's new 'get tough' policy is that its protection can longer be assured.
One outcome may be a move towards solvency ratings on Japanese insurers, such as those issued by Standard & Poor's, Moody's and AM Best and heavily used in the rest of the world's insurance markets.
Another is that, if consumers do start demanding evidence of financial strength before placing their funds, it may open opportunities for foreign life insurers.

Foreign insurers have struggled to compete with the estimated 400,000 out-of-house sales staff, mostly housewives, whose selling success has given Japan the world's highest total contracted life insurance coverage, the highest ratio of insurance to national income and highest insured amount per person.
The Nissan crisis might just give them a chance to market their financial strength, but this is an opening Japan's market leaders are unlikely to put up with for long.
